sentences.text: The genus name Eschatornis blends Greek and Latin roots to mean “last bird,” reflecting its perceived status as the most recent phorusrhacid.
The species epithet aterradora translates as “terrifying,” echoing the common name “terror bird.”
The preserved partial left tibiotarsus—a fused lower leg bone—shows features typical of Phorusrhacidae and resembles members of the subfamilies Psilopterinae and Mesembriornithinae.
Radiometric dating places Eschatornis at roughly 25,326 to 25,733 calibrated years Before Present, potentially extending the phorusrhacid record into the Late Pleistocene.
Carbon isotope analysis indicates the bird inhabited a mesic, arboreal savannah rich in vegetation.
Eschatornis aterradora is known from a single partial left tibiotarsus.
The holotype, specimen MCL-A-1.795, was recovered by Cástor Cartelle in the Toca dos Ossos cave of Bahia, Brazil.
In 2008 Herculano Alvarenga and colleagues tentatively assigned the fossil to an indeterminate member of Cathartidae.
Victor Hugo M. Machado and collaborators formally described the new genus and species in 2026.
Eschatornis belongs to the extinct family Phorusrhacidae, the so-called terror birds.
An oblique supratendinal bridge and an oval opening on the extensor sulcus link the specimen to phorusrhacids rather than to cathartids.
